recipes.name: Blank
recipes.summary: Empty starter recipe. One field, one no-op stage. Replace contents of pipelineDsl with your own simulation.

recipes.name: FitzHugh-Nagumo (example)
recipes.summary: Excitable medium. Fast u spikes through a cubic threshold; slow v recovers and suppresses. Diffusion turns spikes into traveling fronts; an asymmetric seed breaks a front into a rotating spiral.

recipes.name: Belousov-Zhabotinsky (example)
recipes.summary: 3-field oscillating chemistry. u is the fast autocatalyst, v is the medium-timescale inhibitor, w is the slow tertiary recovery. Three timescales produce nested target waves and rotating spirals.

recipes.name: Kuramoto chimera (example)
recipes.summary: Coupled phase oscillators on a sphere. Sakaguchi lag α near π/2 lets sync and chaos coexist; the sphere's closed surface produces rotating-spiral chimera patterns.

recipes.name: Ice-albedo (example)
recipes.summary: Bistable climate. Ice reflects sunlight and stays cold; ocean absorbs it and stays warm. Two stable basins; a perturbation near the threshold can flip the entire planet.

recipes.name: SIR epidemic (example)
recipes.summary: Spatial Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model. Outbreak fronts propagate from seed points and leave a recovered trail behind them; β/γ controls wave speed and final attack rate.

recipes.name: Klausmeier vegetation (example)
recipes.summary: Semi-arid biomass-water dynamics. Vegetation self-organizes into stripes perpendicular to the slope (Sahelian tiger bush). Drop FLOW SPEED to zero and the same kinetics produce Turing spots.

recipes.name: Predator-prey (example)
recipes.summary: Rosenzweig-MacArthur with diffusion. Prey colonizes empty cells, predators follow eating, a void trails the predators which is then re-colonized. Sustained chase-wave limit cycle.

recipes.name: Wave equation (example)
recipes.summary: Hyperbolic wave on a sphere — leapfrog second-order time integration via history fields. Drop a stone, watch the ripple bounce around the sphere forever (γ=0) or decay smoothly (γ>0).

recipes.name: Shallow water (example)
recipes.summary: Depth-averaged fluid on a sphere. gradient(h) drives momentum, divergence(m) drives continuity, dye rides @upstream of the velocity. Drop a height bulge and watch the wave race around the planet, hit the antipode, refocus. Paint dye to see the otherwise-invisible currents.

recipes.name: Vicsek flock (example)
recipes.summary: Emergent flocking on a sphere. Each cell has a heading vec2; each tick it adopts the neighborhood-mean direction plus a random rotation. Below the critical noise the whole sphere polarizes into one color; above it, alignment is frustrated and topological defects drift around. Sweep NOISE η = 0.1 → 0.5 to watch a real second-order phase transition.

recipes.name: Schrödinger packet (example)
recipes.summary: Quantum particle on a sphere — i·dψ/dt = Ĥψ in real and imaginary parts, symplectic leapfrog time stepping. Default scenario releases an eastward Gaussian wavepacket at the equator; watch it disperse, traverse the sphere, hit its own backside, and fill the surface with self-interference caustics. Paint potentials with the WELL or BARRIER stamps to bend the wave.

recipes.name: Cyclic CA (example)
recipes.summary: Each cell holds a state in [0, N). Every tick, if any neighbor is at state (self+1) mod N, the cell advances. Random initial state → self-organized rotating spirals across the whole sphere. The 12 pentagonal cells pin spiral cores, giving the dynamics a permanent topological signature of the substrate. First v2 demo of u32 field types.

recipes.name: Ising model (example)
recipes.summary: Stochastic ferromagnet on a sphere. Each cell stores a spin and explicit RNG state; rand01(rng) proposes Metropolis flips and rngNext(rng) advances the state. Low temperature coarsens into domains, high temperature boils.

recipes.name: SmoothLife metric (example)
recipes.summary: SmoothLife-style continuous cellular automaton using weighted metric kernels. A center-weighted bell kernel estimates inner life; an annular bell kernel estimates the outer environment. Smooth birth/survival windows turn those densities into flowing cellular organisms.

recipes.name: Lenia metric (example)
recipes.summary: Single-channel Lenia on the sphere. A metric bell kernel computes a neighborhood potential by great-circle distance; a Gaussian growth curve nudges each cell up or down. Tune kernel center/width and growth center/width to find soft colonies, holes, and drifting organism-like patches.

recipes.name: Wilson-Cowan neural field (example)
recipes.summary: Excitation-inhibition neural field on a sphere. A narrow metric bell kernel gathers local excitation; a wider annular bell kernel gathers inhibition. The sigmoid firing response turns random seed activity into pulses, labyrinths, and breathing cortical-wave patterns.

recipes.name: Nonlocal ecology (example)
recipes.summary: Resource-biomass ecology with nonlocal competition. Plants read nearby resource through a center-weighted metric kernel, while wider annular biomass creates crowding pressure. The competition radius sets patch spacing, producing gaps, mosaics, and invasion fronts without ordinary diffusion.

recipes.name: Gierer-Meinhardt (example)
recipes.summary: Activator-inhibitor R-D — short-range a²/h amplification, long-range h diffusion. The diffusion contrast crystallizes random noise into Turing spots, stripes, or leopard patterns. Sharper than Gray-Scott because the kinetics are multiplicative rather than competitive.

recipes.name: Brusselator (example)
recipes.summary: Synthetic two-species R-D from Prigogine + Lefever. Steady state u=A, v=B/A; with D_v ≫ D_u the homogeneous fixed point goes Turing-unstable and noise crystallizes into stripes. Cleanest classroom demo of pattern formation.

recipes.name: Lengyel-Epstein CIMA (example)
recipes.summary: Chlorite-iodide-malonic-acid R-D — first experimentally confirmed Turing patterns (Castets et al. 1990). Rational kinetics u·v/(1+u²); the σ stiffness lets the inhibitor's effective timescale outrun the activator's so the Turing condition holds even when raw diffusion coefficients are similar.

recipes.name: Aliev-Panfilov (cardiac, example)
recipes.summary: Modified FitzHugh-Nagumo tuned to cardiac action potentials. State-dependent recovery rate ε(u,v) reproduces restitution and curvature dispersion, which together turn a single plane-wave break into a self-sustaining spiral rotor — the canonical mathematical model of cardiac fibrillation.

recipes.name: Burgers' equation (example)
recipes.summary: Scalar self-advection — du/dt + u·du/dx = ν·∇²u — the simplest PDE that does shock formation. Smooth profiles steepen at their leading edge until viscosity stops the singularity. The NOISE scenario produces Burgers turbulence: a tangled landscape of merging shocks that slowly anneals to a few dominant fronts.

recipes.name: Kobayashi snowflake (example)
recipes.summary: Anisotropic phase-field crystal growth — Kobayashi (1993). A solid seed releases latent heat that warms the surrounding liquid; protrusions cool faster than concavities so the front becomes unstable, and the six-fold ε(θ) anisotropy locks the resulting dendrites into snowflake branches. Drop a single seed and watch a hexagonal snowflake grow on the sphere over ~30 wall-seconds.

recipes.name: Toner-Tu flocking (example)
recipes.summary: Continuum limit of Vicsek-style flocking. Velocity v is self-propelled toward magnitude √(α/β); density ρ is conserved by ∇·(ρv); pressure smooths density bunching, viscosity aligns neighbours. Below the critical noise the whole sphere polarises into a single global flow direction with persistent dense bands (Toner-Tu's giant number fluctuations); above it, flow is turbulent. The continuous-density alternative to the Vicsek-flock recipe.

recipes.name: Drossel-Schwabl forest fire (example)
recipes.summary: Canonical self-organised-criticality CA. Three states per cell — empty / tree / burning. Trees grow from empty cells with probability p; lightning ignites trees with probability f; burning cells spread to tree neighbours and become empty next tick. At small f and p≫f the fire-size distribution is a power law; this is the textbook example of SOC.

recipes.name: BTW sandpile (example)
recipes.summary: Bak-Tang-Wiesenfeld sandpile. Slowly drop grains; when a cell reaches the toppling threshold (6) it loses 6 grains and sends 1 to each neighbour, possibly cascading. The 12 pentagonal cells (5 neighbours) dissipate one grain per topple, so the icosphere self-organises around a critical density set by mass-balance with these pinned defects. SOC by deterministic toppling — complementary to the forest-fire recipe's stochastic-ignition mechanism.

recipes.name: Greenberg-Hastings excitable medium (example)
recipes.summary: Minimal CA model of excitable media. Each cell holds an integer phase: 0 = resting, 1 = excited, 2..K-1 = refractory. Resting cells fire when any neighbour is excited; everything else marches toward rest. Drop a half-wave on the sphere and it closes into a rotating spiral pinned to a pentagonal cell. The discrete-state cousin of FitzHugh-Nagumo.

recipes.name: Eden growth (example)
recipes.summary: Simplest stochastic aggregation. Each empty cell with an occupied neighbour flips to occupied with probability g per tick. From a single seed the cluster expands with a rough advancing front; the icosphere's 12 pentagonal cells subtly perturb the boundary but the bulk grows isotropically. The front roughens as ~t^β before saturating when the cluster wraps the sphere.

recipes.name: Coupled-map lattice (example)
recipes.summary: Per-cell logistic map x' = r·x·(1−x) with diffusive coupling ε to the local mean. At ε=0 every cell is its own chaotic process; at intermediate ε you get Kaneko's spatiotemporal intermittency — frozen random patches that occasionally rupture; at large ε the sphere locks into a coherent oscillator. The only recipe in the catalog using deterministic chaos rather than explicit randomness.
